papers.title: Exploring genetic variants in premature ovarian insufficiency: a cohort-based investigation of monogenic etiologies.
papers.abstract: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), affecting about 3.5% of women under 40, is marked by menstrual irregularities, amenorrhea, and heterogeneous pubertal development. Although next-generation sequencing (NGS) has expanded the list of POI-associated genes, most cases remain unexplained, and the clinical diagnostic value of gene panels is still insufficiently assessed. This study combines a cohort-based analysis with a critical methodological reassessment of NGS diagnostic yield in POI. Prospective multicenter observational cohort study (2016-2023). Three Belgian academic hospitals. One hundred sixty unrelated women with idiopathic POI and 716 female controls. Targeted NGS of 155 POI-associated genes. Variants were classified following American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology guidelines, and genes were evaluated using the latest gene-disease relationship (GDR) scoring framework. Identification of pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants (primary outcome). Diagnostic yield of the gene panel based on genes with strong evidence (secondary outcome). Pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants were identified in 19.3% of patients; however, only 7.5% were considered clinically relevant based on gene validity and inheritance patterns. Limiting analysis to the 40 genes with the strongest GDR evidence yielded a 4.4% diagnostic rate. Adding 10 genes supported by recent literature increased the yield to 7.5%. In patients with primary amenorrhea, the diagnostic rate reached 15.4%. These findings highlight the gap between variant burden and true diagnostic yield in POI. Targeted NGS panels provide valuable clinical insight into POI genetics but should be complemented with broader genomic approaches for comprehensive diagnosis.

papers.title: Integrative Genetic, Transcriptomic, and Single-Cell Analyses Prioritize Druggable Candidate Genes in Knee Osteoarthritis.
papers.abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a common degenerative joint disease with a complex pathogenesis and a lack of effective molecular targets. This study aimed to prioritize druggable genes associated with KOA and investigate their expression patterns and cellular localization by integrating genetic, transcriptomic, and single-cell analyses. We first screened for potential druggable genes genetically associated with KOA using MR analysis. Subsequently, batch-corrected synovial transcriptomic data were analyzed using weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and the genes of the most relevant module were integrated with the MR candidates. A total of 127 machine-learning pipelines were evaluated using repeated nested cross-validation, followed by external validation and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) interpretation. The expression levels of key genes were further validated by experiments. Single-cell RNA sequencing, immune-cell deconvolution, and peripheral immune-cell-specific eQTL-MR were used to investigate the cellular contexts potentially associated with the candidate genes. Finally, potential drug-gene interactions were retrieved from DGIdb, and selected target-compound pairs were evaluated using molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations. A total of 315 druggable genes showed nominal MR associations with KOA. After integrating KOA-associated WGCNA module, we identified 15 candidate genes. Next, the random forest was selected as the optimal machine-learning model, achieving a mean outer-cross-validation AUC of 0.929 (95% CI, 0.913-0.945). SHAP and differential-expression analyses prioritized four genes. JUN, ADAMTS1, and CRISPLD2 were downregulated in KOA synovium, whereas CX3CR1 was upregulated, and these expression patterns were supported by experimental validation. Single-cell analysis revealed that JUN, ADAMTS1, and CRISPLD2 were predominantly expressed in fibroblast-related populations and CX3CR1 was mainly expressed in myeloid cells, with their expression varying across fibroblast and macrophage states. Peripheral immune-cell-specific eQTL-MR identified nominal associations for JUN in plasma cells, ADAMTS1 in NK_R cells, and CX3CR1 in NK cells. However, none remained significant after correction for multiple testing. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations showed that the ADAMTS1-pravastatin and CX3CR1-Rugocrixan complexes maintained stable protein-ligand contacts during their respective simulations. Integrative multi-omics analyses identified JUN, ADAMTS1, CRISPLD2, and CX3CR1 as prioritized candidate genes associated with KOA. These genes were associated with distinct states of synovial fibroblasts and myeloid cells. These findings provide a foundation for further mechanistic validation and experimental evaluation of candidate drug-target interactions.

papers.title: Artificial neural network data fusion-mediated dual-mode sensor based on Fe 3 O 4 @PdIr for Salmonellatyphimurium detection in food.
papers.abstract: Salmonella Typhimurium (S. typhimurium) is a major foodborne pathogen that poses a serious threat to public health. In this study, a colorimetric/electrochemical dual-mode biosensor assisted by artificial neural network (ANN) was developed for the sensitive detection of S. typhimurium. Fe 3 O 4 @PdIr nanocomposites with enhanced peroxidase-like activity and electrochemical performance were prepared and conjugated with an aptamer specific to S. typhimurium to obtain Fe 3 O 4 @PdIr-Apt. Through the sandwich binding of Fe 3 O 4 @PdIr-Apt and Apt to the target, the nanocomposites were attached to microplates or Au electrodes, thereby generating colorimetric and electrochemical signals. The ANN model deeply resolved the complex nonlinear relationship between the dual signals, enabling mutual correction and ultimately performing data fusion to output a single detection result, which significantly reduced the mean square error while improving detection sensitivity and reliability. This sensor exhibited a wide linear range of 2.7-2.7 × 10 8 CFU/mL and a low detection limit of 1.66 CFU/mL. Additionally, this method was successfully applied to the detection of S. typhimurium in pork and milk, with a recovery rate of 95.19% ∼ 104.07%. It indicated that the constructed sensor holds great practical potential for S. typhimurium detection.

papers.title: Purification and identification of lipid-lowering peptides from Tartary buckwheat protein and study on the mechanism of lipid-lowering activity.
papers.abstract: Highly active lipid-lowering peptides were isolated from Tartary buckwheat through enzymatic hydrolysis, ultrafiltration, and reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC). Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and molecular docking techniques were employed to identify and screen lipid-lowering peptide monomers. The lipid-lowering effects and underlying mechanisms were evaluated through molecular docking visualization, in vitro chemical assays, the 3 T3-L1 cell model, and the Caenorhabditis elegans(C. elegans) model. Five novel peptides were identified: FHWDYPQA, FHWDYPQALE, LFHWDYPQA, LPSYSNAPYI, and NAIIGPRW. These peptides bind to receptor proteins 1LPB and 1F6W via hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic interactions. These peptides significantly inhibited pancreatic lipase activity, effectively reduced lipid accumulation in 3 T3-L1 cells, and lowered triglycerides (TG), total cholesterol (TC), and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels. In addition, LI-10, FE-10, and LA-9 significantly elevated high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDLC) levels. Additionally, five peptides effectively reduced lipid accumulation in high-fat-fed C. elegans, decreased TG, glucose (GLU), and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels. Overall, these findings elucidate the lipid-lowering mechanisms of five novel peptides identified from Tartary buckwheat protein hydrolysates, providing a scientific foundation for the future development of Tartary buckwheat protein-derived functional products targeting hyperlipidemia.

papers.title: Lineage-aware comparative genomics shows no consistent reservoir-specific plasmidome in low-moisture food associated Salmonella Enteritidis.
papers.abstract: Foodborne outbreaks of Salmonella Enteritidis have been historically linked to poultry, but outbreaks associated with low-moisture foods (LMFs) are increasingly reported. Since plasmids encode stress-response and tolerance traits that support persistence in dry environments, this study evaluated whether LMF-associated (nuts, spices, grains, etc.) S. enteritidis isolates carry lineage-specific plasmidomes distinct from non-LMF (poultry/egg-associated and production-environment). A total of 2824 non-clinical records were curated from the NCBI Pathogen Detection database and organized into 51 SNP clusters (30 non-LMF, 11 LMF, 10 mixed). Reservoir comparisons were restricted to mixed clusters (319 non-LMF, 24 LMF at the metadata level) using 64 assemblies (24 LMF, 40 non-LMF). PlasmidFinder identified that most genomes contained IncF plasmid (IncFIB(S) 90.6%, IncFII(S) 89.1%), though global Fisher's exact tests and lineage-stratified CMH tests (FDR-adjusted) identified no replicon family enriched in LMF. MOB-suite reconstructed 88 plasmids from 63/64 genomes and assigned 11 backbone clusters dominated by AB461 (58/64 genomes). Plasmid counts, mobility profiles, and functional annotations were similar across reservoirs, with variations attributable to SNP clusters rather than isolation source. In the largest mixed lineage (PDS000218745.3; 9 LMF, 15 controls), no LMF-enriched plasmid gene products were detected. Shared accessory plasmids occurred in both reservoirs, including AB233 carrying mer operon genes and emrE, while rare LMF-only backbones (AB947; AA149; AA372 encoding TEM β-lactamase, toxN, mbeA, proQ) were isolate-specific. Pangenome analysis of 4899 gene clusters likewise found no accessory genes significantly enriched in LMF after lineage-stratified testing. Plasmid architecture was largely lineage-structured with limited evidence for association with LMF environments.

papers.title: When "dead" isn't dead: VBNC entering and survival modeling of Salmonella Typhimurium ATCC 14028 in low-water-activity conditions.
papers.abstract: Salmonella can persist in low water activity (a w ) foods for years. This high resistance to conservation methods applied by the food industry makes this pathogen a public health concern. In this work, a predictive model to describe the survival of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium ATCC 14028 under four different water activity (0.9, 0.8, 0.7 and 0.6 a w ) conditions was determined, in parallel with the determination of cell viability throughout and after exposure to stress to monitor the entry and persistence of this pathogen in the VBNC state. In addition, morphological changes in the cells at the beginning of the stress, before and after the loss of culturability, and on the last day of exposure to stress were analyzed. The Weibull model best described the survival of Salmonella Typhimurium under the tested conditions. Even after Salmonella Typhimurium reached the detection limits, viable cells were detected, indicating the presence of cells in the VBNC state. The population in the VBNC state was gradually formed throughout the exposure to stress, corresponding to all viable cells quantified by flow cytometry and visualized by fluorescence microscopy at the end of 30 and 45 days. Cells exposed at 0.6 a w had a significant increase in cellular length, reaching 185% higher length size than the no stressed cells. The fact that the pathogen shows a relatively slow inactivation rate in highly osmotic environments and remains viable, even when it is undetectable by conventional techniques, may became Salmonella more resistant and promote its entrance into a VBNC state.

papers.title: Listeria monocytogenes dry surface biofilms: a comparative study of mono- and coculture with Enterococcus faecium.
papers.abstract: Dry surface biofilms (DSB) represent a challenge for microbial control in the food industry, since they show high desiccation resistance. This study evaluated the formation, viability, and composition of Listeria monocytogenes DSB in mono- and coculture with Enterococcus faecium. DSB were formed on polypropylene (PP) and stainless steel (SS) coupons using two hydrated-dry cycling protocols: P1 (48/48 h) and P2 (24/120 h), followed by storage (25 °C) for 42 days. At the forming endpoint (day 0), in DSB mono-species, Listeria monocytogenes was ca. 2 log CFU/cm 2 higher on PP than on SS (p = 5.1 e-05). The pathogen remained viable for up to 42 days, but with reductions of ≥1.7 log CFU/cm 2 , compared to day 0. In dual-species DSB, Enterococcus faecium inhibited Listeria monocytogenes regardless of surface or protocol, maintaining pathogen levels at or below the detection limit (1.4 log CFU/cm 2 ) throughout storage. Meanwhile, Enterococcus faecium achieved 5 log CFU/cm 2 on day 0 and 3.4 log CFU/cm 2 after 42 days. In addition, catalase treatment resuscitated VBNC Listeria monocytogenes cells on day 0 and within 14 days of storage, increasing culturability by up to 1.0 log CFU/cm 2 . In general, DSB matrices contained higher protein levels than carbohydrates and eDNA, and Listeria monocytogenes exhibited morphological alterations, including elongation and L-form-like cells. Overall, these findings highlight the need for strict hygiene measures to control DSB and suggest that Enterococcus faecium may be an effective strategy to inhibit the Listeria monocytogenes DSB formation.

papers.title: LMP2A Promotes Immune Escape by Regulating PD-L1 Expression via the PI3K/AKT/STAT3 Axis in EBV-Positive Gastric Cancer.
papers.abstract: LMP2A, a key Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-encoded protein, is closely associated with viral oncogenesis. However, its role in modulating PD-L1 expression and mediating immune escape in EBV-positive gastric cancer (EBVaGC) remains incompletely clarified. This research sought to elucidate the functional effect and molecular mechanism of LMP2A in EBVaGC. Functional experiments involving LMP2A overexpression and silencing were conducted to evaluate this influence on cellular proliferation (using CCK-8 and EdU incorporation assays), immune evasion (via co-culture with CD8 + T cells followed by TUNEL apoptosis assay and ELISA for Granzyme B and Perforin), and PD-L1 expression. The participation of the PI3K/AKT/STAT3 axis was evaluated using western blot and rescue experiments employing the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 and activator 740 Y-P. Furthermore, dual epistatic rescue experiments combining PD-L1 siRNA knockdown and PI3K pathway intervention were performed to verify the upstream-downstream relationship. In vivo findings were validated using a subcutaneous xenograft model. LMP2A and PD-L1 were higher in EBVaGC cell lines than EBV-negative gastric cancer (EBVnGC). Forced expression of LMP2A in EBVnGC cells enhanced proliferative capacity and reduced susceptibility to CD8 + T cell-mediated cytotoxicity, and increased PD-L1 level. Pharmacological rescue experiments confirmed that LMP2A activated the PI3K/AKT/STAT3 axis to modulate cell proliferation and PD-L1-mediated immune escape. Notably, further epistatic verification experiments demonstrated that PD-L1 knockdown completely abolished the phenotypic changes induced by PI3K pathway modulation, eliminating the possibility of feedback regulation and confirming that PD-L1 acts as the mandatory direct downstream effector of the PI3K/AKT/STAT3 axis. In vivo xenograft experiments further validated that LMP2A facilitated tumor growth and PD-L1 upregulation via PI3K/AKT/STAT3 signaling. LMP2A upregulates PD-L1 expression and promotes immune escape in EBVaGC by activating the PI3K/AKT/STAT3 axis. These findings offer a new theoretical foundation and potential interventional targets for improving immunotherapeutic outcomes in EBVaGC.

papers.title: CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS AND OUTCOMES IN ADULTS WITH BACTERIAL MENINGITIS AND NEGATIVE CEREBROSPINAL FLUID CULTURES.
papers.abstract: Ten to thirty percent of patients with bacterial meningitis have negative CSF cultures, yet their clinical characteristics and outcome remain poorly defined. Between 2006 and 2023, adults with bacterial meningitis were prospectively included in a nationwide cohort study. Patients with negative CSF cultures were compared to those with positive CSF cultures. Outcome was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale, with scores of 1-4 classified as unfavourable. CSF samples from microbiology-negative patients underwent additional testing with the IS-pro assay, a broad-spectrum PCR technique. CSF cultures were negative in 413 of 3,132 episodes (13%). A pathogen was identified in 328 (80%) through blood culture, CSF bacterial PCR, or antigen testing, leaving 85 episodes without microbiological confirmation. Patients with negative CSF cultures more often received pre-admission antibiotics (13% vs 10%, p=0.02) and had lower rates of unfavourable outcome (29% vs 39%, p<0.001). Blood cultures were positive in 53%, and CSF PCR detected a pathogen in 49%. The IS-pro assay detected Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=5), Streptococcus bovis group/Streptococcus intermedius (n=5), and Streptococcus constellatus (n=1). Bacterial meningitis patients with negative CSF cultures have more favourable outcomes. Combining CSF cultures with blood cultures and CSF PCR improves pathogen detection, while broad-spectrum PCR may help identify atypical pathogens.

papers.title: Scallops as an emerging platform toward functional reproductive endocrinology.
papers.abstract: Scallops have become one of the few molluscan systems in which reproductive endocrinology can be examined beyond descriptive molecular surveys. This review summarizes a series of studies that have progressively positioned scallops as an emerging experimental platform for advancing functional approaches in comparative reproductive endocrinology. Early work identified GnRH/CRZ-superfamily peptides and their receptors in scallops, showing that these ancient neuropeptide-GPCR modules are present in bivalves and may have multifunctional roles, but should not be interpreted as direct counterparts of the vertebrate hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Molecular analyses of sterol-related and nuclear-receptor-related pathways, together with sex-identification markers, further suggest that scallops provide a useful system for examining candidate mechanisms associated with gametogenesis, sex differentiation, and the stable maintenance of sexual phenotypes, without assuming vertebrate-type sex steroid regulation. At the cellular level, studies of germ cells and gonadal somatic cells have revealed the importance of the gonadal niche, whereas scallop hemocytes have emerged as experimentally accessible primary cells for cellular-level functional assays, rather than as established reproductive endocrine target cells. A major technical breakthrough has been the discovery and application of a strong OsHV-1 promoter, which has enabled transient transgene expression in scallop cells. Combined with primary hemocyte culture, this system has supported subcellular localization assays, recombinant protein production, and functional assessment of genes of interest, thereby providing a complementary route to gene function analysis in bivalves where individual-based functional genetics remains difficult. Despite current limitations, including low transfection efficiency, interindividual variability, and the limited extrapolation of hemocyte-based phenotypes to gonadal or organism-level reproductive physiology, scallop cell-based platforms provide a promising foundation for hypothesis-driven comparative endocrinology. These advances illustrate how non-model molluscs can be developed from observational subjects into experimentally testable systems, offering new perspectives on endocrine evolution, reproductive regulation, and physiological integration in marine invertebrates.

papers.title: Discovering multi-omics predictors for lithium response in bipolar disorder by integrating proteomic and genomic data: A 6-month follow-up study.
papers.abstract: Reliable predictors of lithium response in bipolar disorder (BD) are unavailable, and reported predictors have rarely been temporally validated. We examined whether baseline proteomic, clinical, and polygenic information predicts lithium response using a temporal validation design. Patients with BD from three hospitals were assessed over six months (acute) or at baseline (stable maintenance); lithium response was rated with the Alda scale. Of 295 participants with complete multi-omic data, 228 in the acute phase entered prediction analyses: elastic-net models (responders, Alda A ≥ 7) developed in an earlier cohort (n = 110) were applied to a later, separately assayed validation cohort (n = 118). In the validation cohort, the protein model showed modest discrimination (AUC = 0.58, 95% CI 0.47-0.70; permutation p = 0.060), whereas clinical (AUC = 0.51) and polygenic (AUC = 0.46) models did not transfer, and combining modalities did not improve prediction. In an exploratory comparison of clear responders and non-responders (Alda A ≥ 7 vs ≤3), protein models reached AUC 0.67-0.70. Protein discrimination was similar with validation-blind preprocessing but weaker in sensitivity analyses. Validation was temporal rather than site-independent, and most patients were already taking lithium at baseline sampling. Under temporal validation, baseline proteomic profiles carried at most modest information about lithium response, and clinical and polygenic predictors did not transfer. Candidate markers need external validation in larger cohorts sampled before lithium initiation.

papers.title: A High-Sensitivity RPA/Cas12a Assay for Rapid Detection of the Select Agent Ralstonia solanacearum R3b2.
papers.abstract: Ralstonia solanacearum is a globally distributed, soil-borne species complex that causes bacterial wilt in many economically important crops. Race 3 biovar 2 (R3b2) is a cold-tolerant, highly aggressive subgroup within this complex that is responsible for an estimated $1 billion in annual global losses. Because R3b2 remains exotic to North America, it is classified as a USDA Select Agent due to its high potential to devastate U.S. solanaceous crops and ornamental industries. However, current diagnostic methods for this pathogen involve trade-offs among cost, sensitivity, specificity, and ease of use, particularly for point-of-care (POC) detection in field settings. CRISPR-based detection platforms have recently emerged as promising tools for high-sensitivity POC diagnostics. Here we developed an isothermal recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA)/Cas12a assay for specific, sensitive and rapid detection of R3b2. By targeting a genomic region associated with the cool-virulence phenotype, the assay reliably differentiates R3b2 from plant hosts and other diverse R. solanacearum strains. Incorporation of a dual-guide RNA system and an 8-mer single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) fluorescent reporter further improved sensitivity and reduced detection time. Using dilution series of R3b2-spiked Pelargonium DNA extracts, the assay detected as few as 4 CFU per reaction. To facilitate POC applications, the system was adapted into a one-pot, contamination-resistan¬t format compatible with portable fluorescence readers such as Genie III device and P51 viewer. By improving both sensitivity and portability, this assay enhances current diagnostic capabilities and, pending validation in real-world conditions, supports early surveillance efforts aimed at preventing the introduction of R3b2 into the United States.

papers.title: Microfluidic-Based Molecular Diagnostics for Pathogen Detection in Urine Samples for Resource-Limited Settings: A Review.
papers.abstract: Urine is a convenient, noninvasive specimen for molecular diagnostics, offering advantages in scalability, patient compliance, and suitability for decentralized testing. However, its clinical adoption for molecular pathogen detection remains limited by intrinsic physicochemical variability, low target abundance, and the presence of inhibitors of enzymatic nucleic acid amplification that may seriously compromise assay sensitivity and reproducibility. In this review, we introduce a urine-first design paradigm in which device architecture and assay chemistry are codesigned around the unique biochemical constraints of urine rather than adapted from conventional blood-based workflows. This paradigm is built on three interdependent principles: matrix-aware sample processing with efficient inhibitor removal and multifraction nucleic acid capture; amplification chemistry with built-in tolerance to pH fluctuations, ionic variability, and residual urinary inhibitors; and closed, integrated microfluidic architectures that minimize contamination risk. We compare on-chip amplification strategies, including PCR, isothermal amplification methods such as LAMP and RPA, digital PCR, and CRISPR-assisted detection, and evaluate trade-offs in sensitivity, inhibitor tolerance, and deployability. Detection modalities, including fluorescence, colorimetric, electrochemical, and lateral-flow readouts, are assessed for analytical performance and compatibility with resource-limited settings. By integrating biological insight with engineering design, this review provides a practical roadmap for developing accessible, field-ready urine-based diagnostic platforms.

papers.title: Are We Going to the Dogs? Human Disease Phenotypes in Canines.
papers.abstract: Companion dogs are increasingly recognized as translational models for studying human physiology and disease. Unlike conventional or genetically engineered laboratory models, dogs are outbred, immunocompetent animals that spontaneously develop complex diseases whose pathogenesis and environmental exposures commonly overlap with those of humans. These distinctive features create opportunities to study mechanisms of disease, progression, and therapeutic responses under conditions that more closely resemble clinical reality. This review highlights evidence for the translational relevance of canine models across multiple therapeutic areas. We further discuss how advances in genomics, transcriptomics, spatial biology, and in vitro and in silico model systems are expanding the translational utility of canine models for applications in human medicine. Although important species differences must be carefully weighed, dogs represent a uniquely valuable comparative model for elucidating disease mechanisms, informing drug development, and accelerating the translation of scientific discoveries to human medicine.

papers.title: Molecular Detection of Cryptosporidium spp. in Coypu (Myocastor coypus) in China: Genetic Diversity and Zoonotic Potential.
papers.abstract: Cryptosporidium is a globally important enteric pathogen commonly reported in rodents. The coypu (Myocastor coypus) is a large rodent adapted to semi-aquatic environments and is increasingly farmed as a fur-bearing animal. To assess the occurrence and zoonotic potential of Cryptosporidium in farmed coypus across China, a total of 308 faecal samples were collected from seven cities and screened via PCR targeting the small subunit (SSU) rRNA gene. Positive samples were further analysed with nested PCR targeting the 60-kDa glycoprotein (gp60) gene. The overall infection rate was 8.8% (27/308), with city-level prevalence ranging from 0% (0/22) to 19.4% (19/98). Four distinct Cryptosporidium species/genotypes were identified: C. ubiquitum (n = 15), C. myocastoris (n = 5), C. parvum (n = 1), and the Cryptosporidium deer mouse genotype IV (n = 6). Further subtyping classified the C. parvum isolate as IIaA18G1R1 (n = 1) and revealed a novel C. ubiquitum subtype family, designated XIIk (n = 13). Phylogenetically, XIIk clustered with the zoonotic XIIa group. These results reveal the genetic diversity of Cryptosporidium in farmed coypus and highlight the need for further investigation of its zoonotic potential.

papers.title: Understanding Trade-Offs Between Modeling Approaches to Forecast Plant Disease Spread and Risk.
papers.abstract: Modeling disease spread and risk is crucial for disease management, with numerous options for models. Multiple factors affect model selection, including the model's spatial and temporal dimensions, the quantity and quality of infection data, management objectives, and the research questions being addressed. We developed a workflow to filter model types based on pathogen biology and infection data availability, then select the appropriate model for the research question and management objectives. We applied the workflow to two case study pathosystems (late blight and sudden oak death) and evaluated three modeling approaches representing different spatial and temporal dimensions: a temporally focused weather-risk model (WRM), a spatially focused species distribution model (SDM), and a spatiotemporal spread model, the Pest or Pathogen Spread (PoPS) model. We qualitatively compared how each model's spatiotemporal outputs affected predicted disease risk or spread. Additionally, we conducted a simulation study in which infection data were reduced to determine the minimum data density required to obtain reliable parameter estimates with PoPS. Our results suggest that the temporal WRM model is suitable for disease management in agricultural pathosystems, where stakeholders possess sufficient spatial knowledge. In the natural pathosystem, the spatiotemporal model's greater accuracy reduced the total high-risk infection area by >99% compared with the other models. We found that although a spatiotemporal model is more accurate and helps with resource allocation, performance dropped significantly when data density fell below 50%. The effect of decreasing data density on SDM performance varied with pathosystem. Our work underscores the need for scalable disease-detection methods.

papers.title: Multilocus Characterization of Podosphaera fragariae Causing Strawberry Powdery Mildew in Lima, Peru: Evidence from ITS, GAPDH, and RPB2 Phylogeny.
papers.abstract: Powdery mildew associated with Fragaria × ananassa Duch. has recently been reinterpreted as a species complex comprising Podosphaera fragariae in Eurasia and P. shepherdiae in the Americas; however, molecular data for South American populations remain scarce, and the few South American specimens sequenced to date have been assigned to P. shepherdiae . In this study, the causal agent of powdery mildew on strawberry cultivar 'Sabrina' grown in Lima, Peru, was characterized through morphological analysis, pathogenicity tests, and multilocus phylogenetic inference based on ITS, GAPDH , and RPB2 . The fungal material examined developed mycelial colonies typical of powdery mildew and consistently reproduced the symptoms observed in the field. Morphologically, the pathogen exhibited characteristics consistent with Podosphaera sect. Sphaerotheca , including ellipsoidal conidia with conspicuous fibrosin bodies, chained conidiogenesis, and Fibroidium -type lateral germination. Sequences were obtained for ITS, GAPDH , and RPB2 . The concatenated ITS+ GAPDH + RPB2 phylogeny resolved two major lineages corresponding to P. fragariae (95%) and P. shepherdiae (98%), placing the Peruvian isolate PUCP-Pa001 within the P. fragariae clade with high statistical support and close affinity to Eurasian accessions. These results provide the first multilocus evidence of P. fragariae on cultivated strawberry in the Americas and support the hypothesis of an anthropogenic introduction associated with the international movement of propagative material. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the value of multilocus approaches for resolving cryptic taxa within Erysiphaceae and provides the first South American reference sequences for this pathogen, supporting future epidemiological and phytosanitary research on powdery mildews associated with Fragaria in South America.

papers.title: QTL Mapping and Genomic Prediction of Disease Reactions of Rice to the Rice Blast Fungus M. oryzae Races.
papers.abstract: Blast disease of rice caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae is one of the most damaging diseases of rice worldwide. Major blast resistance genes have been deployed for broad-spectrum resistance. However, the minor genes and epistatic interactions contributing to the broad-spectrum resistance are largely uncharacterized. Using a mapping population of 272 individuals derived from the blast resistant variety 'Katy' and blast susceptible 'PI312777', we identified and verified resistance spectra of major genes Pi-ta/Ptr and Pi-ks and further identified one additional major and 13 minor resistance quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for 10 of the 11 pathogen races tested and detected additive-by-additive epistasis for 32 pairs of QTLs. We used Bayesian network (BN) structure learning to model associations between QTLs, blast resistance, and agronomic traits, revealing four traits associated with resistance to specific pathogen races. The major gene cluster Pita/Ptr conferred resistance to only 7 of 11 races, highlighting the need for multiple smaller effect resistance QTL to achieve broad-spectrum resistance. Genomic predictive abilities (GPAs) were calculated and were lowest for resistance to race IE1k (for which Pita/Ptr is not effective) and highest for IA45. Reciprocal GPAs were calculated for prediction across pairs of blast races and were lowest for pathogen races IB1, ID1 and IE1k, moderate for races IB49, IE1, IB54, IH1 and highest among IC17, IG1, IA45, IB45. A genomic selection rank sum index (GSRI) of genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs) for overall resistance to 11 pathogen races distinctly separated high and low resistant lines for all races except IE1k.

papers.title: Genomic characterization of greenhouse-associated Aspergillus fumigatus from China reveals population structure, antifungal resistance, and relationships with global lineages.
papers.abstract: Aspergillus fumigatus is a globally distributed saprophyte and a major opportunistic pathogen causing invasive aspergillosis. The emergence of azole-resistant A. fumigatus in agricultural environments poses a growing threat to human health, yet the genetic basis of resistance and the role of agricultural hotspots remain poorly understood. Here, we analyzed 226 greenhouse-derived isolates from Yunnan, China, within a global genomic framework. Although Yunnan isolates shared overall diversity patterns with worldwide populations, they exhibited pronounced population structure, with one well-supported clade (Clade B) enriched in greenhouse environments. To investigate cross-environment relationships, we further analyzed an expanded collection of isolates from greenhouse soils, air, agricultural markets, and clinical sources using multilocus genotyping. Identical or highly similar genotypes were detected across environments, including resistant strains carrying the TR₃₄/L98H allele, demonstrating that greenhouse and clinical isolates are genetically connected. Genome-wide association analyses identified candidate loci associated with antifungal resistance and stress tolerance beyond canonical cyp51A mutations, including genes involved in cell wall remodeling and mitochondrial dynamics. Together, these results reveal the genomic landscape of greenhouse-associated A. fumigatus in China and provide evidence for genetic connectivity between agricultural and clinical settings, underscoring the importance of surveillance at agricultural-clinical interfaces. Azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus is an increasing global health concern because resistant infections are difficult to treat and often fatal. Agricultural environments have been implicated as important sources of resistance, yet the mechanisms underlying the emergence, persistence, and transfer of resistance to human patients remain unclear. By integrating genomic and phenotypic analyses of greenhouse-derived isolates from Yunnan, China, we identified a distinct clade that is enriched in greenhouse environments and exhibits stable antifungal resistance. Resistant genotypes were repeatedly detected across greenhouses, local markets, and patients; notably, identical multilocus genotypes and cyp51A mutations were shared between market air samples and a patient with invasive aspergillosis, demonstrating genetic connectivity between agricultural and clinical settings. Beyond the well-known cyp51A mutations, genome-wide association analyses highlighted several candidate loci associated with antifungal resistance-including a dynamin-related GTPase and a strongly induced cell-wall peptidase-that may represent non-canonical resistance mechanisms. These findings provide insights into fungal adaptation and resistance evolution in agricultural contexts. They underscore the urgent need for integrated surveillance and stewardship across agricultural and medical sectors to mitigate the spread of antifungal resistance.

papers.title: Comparative evaluation of commercial gradient diffusion and disk diffusion tests for aztreonam-avibactam susceptibility testing.
papers.abstract: Aztreonam-avibactam (AZA) is a recently approved agent active against metallo-β-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales. However, independent evaluations of commercially available antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) products remain limited. We evaluated 56 carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales isolates using four newly available AZA AST products, including two gradient diffusion tests (bioMérieux Etest; Liofilchem MIC Test Strip) and two disk diffusion tests (Hardy, Liofilchem) across three Mueller-Hinton agar manufacturers at two independent clinical laboratories. A diverse isolate collection enriched for nonsusceptible and breakpoint-adjacent MICs was used to rigorously assess categorical agreement (CA). Broth microdilution (BMD) was used as the reference method. Essential agreement (EA), categorical agreement, error rates, and reproducibility were analyzed. All four commercial AST products demonstrated acceptable analytical performance compared with reference BMD. Gradient diffusion demonstrated high EA (bioMérieux 92.6%, Liofilchem 89.6%), whereas CA ranged from 81.5% to 89.3% across all four products. Minor errors accounted for all categorical discrepancies and occurred almost exclusively among breakpoint-adjacent isolates. Medium-related variability was modest, and quality control (QC) performance was generally high, with strong within-site precision and consistent performance across laboratories. This study provides the first comprehensive head-to-head comparison of commercial AZA susceptibility testing products and supports their implementation in clinical microbiology laboratories.IMPORTANCEAztreonam-avibactam is an important new treatment option for infections caused by carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, particularly metallo-β-lactamase-producing organisms, but its clinical use requires reliable susceptibility testing. We provide the first head-to-head evaluation of four newly available commercial gradient and disk diffusion products across two independent laboratories and three Mueller-Hinton agar manufacturers. By using a diverse isolate collection enriched for MICs near clinical breakpoints, we also subjected these products to a stringent assessment of categorical agreement. Gradient diffusion demonstrated high essential agreement, and no major or very major errors remained after repeat and discrepancy testing with any product. These findings provide timely, practical evidence to guide clinical laboratories implementing aztreonam-avibactam susceptibility testing.

papers.title: dictyBase 2026: a reimplementation of the Dictyostelium model organism database on minimal infrastructure.
papers.abstract: Dictyostelium discoideum is a model organism used to investigate a wide array of biological processes including chemotaxis, cell motility, phagocytosis, multicellular development, and autophagy. Many of its genes have human orthologs implicated in disease, making it a useful model organism for studying conditions ranging from cancer to neurodegeneration. dictyBase has served this community for two decades as a home for genomic data, protocols, a stock center, and community news. Here we describe a complete reimplementation of dictyBase as a self-contained service that uses static data files rather than a database server. Each gene record gathers curated function, human-disease context, developmental expression, and protein structure in a single webpage. The site also provides tools for sequence search, genome browsing, enrichment analysis, and experimental design. The complete Dicty Stock Center catalog of 7055 strains and 1265 plasmids is included, and both can be ordered from the site. New literature is curated by an author-in-the-loop pipeline. A language model drafts the annotations, the authors of the paper correct them, and a curator approves them. Analyses can be run on curator-approved annotations alone or extended to include those still awaiting review. dictyBase is freely available at https://dicty.org.

papers.title: Dual-Modal Localized Surface Plasmon Resonance Biosensor for Rapid Bacterial Gram-Typing and Species Identification in Bronchoalveolar Lavage Fluid.
papers.abstract: Rapid pathogen identification is critical for timely antibiotic therapy in patients with pneumonia, yet current methods remain too slow or complex for routine clinical use. Here, we describe a localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR)-based biosensor platform that detects Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria directly in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) without nucleic acid extraction or amplification. Gold nano-islands (AuNIs) functionalized with antibodies against lipoteichoic acid (LTA) or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) enabled selective bacterial capture. The sensor achieved a refractive index resolution of 8.52 × 10-8 RIU with good reusability and dynamic range. Detection limits reached the concentration of 0.027 μM for purified LTA and 0.208 endotoxin units (EU) for LPS. When tested with Escherichia coli in artificial samples, the LPS sensor showed a reproducibility standard deviation (RSD) of 3.14%, detecting bacterial growth significantly earlier than conventional OD600 measurement. In 33 clinical BALF samples, sensor results correlated strongly with standard diagnostics (Pearson r = 0.963) and distinguished infected from noninfected cases using cutoff values of 0.060 rad (Gram-positive) and 0.083 rad (Gram-negative). The platform detects polymyxin B susceptibility 8 h earlier than conventional OD600 measurements, and a proof-of-concept sandwich immunoassay enables species-level discrimination between E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. With excellent reproducibility (RSD = 3.14%), reusability over six cycles (84.21% ± 2.03% signal retention), and four-week storage stability (98.63% ± 5.42%), this LSPR platform offers a practical, rapid approach for frontline bacterial screening and accelerated antibiotic stewardship in pneumonia.

papers.title: Emerging advances in multimodal AI in cancer immunotherapy: from multi-scale data integration to clinical decision support.
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy is increasingly reshaping the therapeutic landscape of clinical oncology by inducing effective tumor regression and durable responses in various types of human cancers. However, a substantial fraction of patients resist immunotherapy, or even experience relapse after an initial response. Clinically, the conventional biomarkers often exhibit limited predictive accuracy and poor transferability across tumor types. These limitations highlight the urgent need for more robust, data-driven strategies to decipher tumor-immune dynamics and guide personalized treatment. Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative paradigm in immuno-oncology, offering scalable solutions to decode high-dimensional and heterogeneous biomedical data. The evolution of AI can be broadly divided into six key stages: early machine learning (ML) classifiers, unsupervised representation learning, graph-based modeling of cell-cell interactions, multimodal foundation and biomedical language models, reinforcement and active learning paradigms, and AI virtual cells. At the molecular level, AI facilitates the integration of genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and spatially resolved single-cell omics, supporting fine-grained reconstruction of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). At the clinical interface, the application of deep learning (DL) in liquid biopsy, digital pathology, and radiologic imaging has advanced response prediction, biomarker discovery, and early detection of immune-related adverse events (irAEs), driving personized immunotherapy. This review synthesizes recent progress in AI-guided precision immunotherapy across molecular, cellular, and phenotypic area. By outlining key methodological advances and translational opportunities, we highlight that multimodal AI frameworks can pave the way toward the more interpretable, robust, and individualized immunotherapy strategies for cancer treatment.

papers.title: "Stick-and-Sense": a flexible paper SERS tape for rapid, selective and high - sensitivity food and water pathogen detection.
papers.abstract: Rapid detection of foodborne pathogens is vital for public health, yet conventional methods for identifying Escherichia coli are slow, costly, and laboratory dependent. We present a simple paper-based SERS sensor fabricated by coating commercial adhesive tape with self-assembled gold nanoparticles. The platform enables label-free discrimination of E. coli, Enterococcus, and Citrobacter in water using their characteristic Raman fingerprints and principal component analysis, achieving a calculated E. coli detection limit of 26 CFU/mL. To operate in complex food matrices, the substrate was functionalized with an anti-E. coli antibody, enabling selective detection in commercial milk at concentrations as low as 25 CFU/mL, thereby experimentally validating the sensor performance in a real food matrix. Compared to existing flexible SERS substrates, our dual-mode approach combining label-free identification in aqueous media with targeted immunodetection in food offers competitive sensitivity, straightforward fabrication, and an enhancement factor of ≈10 7 . These results highlight the potential of this paper-based SERS sensor as an accessible tool for rapid, on-site microbial monitoring in both water and food safety applications.

papers.title: Exploratory Three-Year Field Assessment of Trichoderma -Colonized Mulch for Managing Armillaria mellea in Vineyards.
papers.abstract: Sustainable management of the fungus Armillaria mellea (white root rot) in viticulture is hindered by the lack of effective chemical treatments and quantitative diagnostic tools. This study adopts a circular economy perspective by repurposing spent mushroom substrate colonized by Trichoderma , a prevalent local industrial by-product, as an organic mulch. We hypothesized that this colonized substrate, selected for the aggressive mycoparasitic capabilities and competitive niche exclusion of Trichoderma , could mitigate pathogen expansion and support vine longevity. The objective was to evaluate the impact of this Trichoderma -colonized mulch on pathogen expansion compared with (i) an untreated control (no mulch) and (ii) an identical composted substrate without T . harzianum . Over a 3-year field assessment using a nonreplicated, single-plot-per-treatment design in a commercial vineyard ( Vitis vinifera ), the system was evaluated through longitudinal visual health monitoring and a newly developed qPCR framework using novel species-specific primers and a probe for A . mellea . The qPCR framework was applied to a subset of the data and therefore provided limited treatment-level evidence. Initially healthy plants under Trichoderma -colonized mulch ( n = 271) showed high health retention (81.2%), comparable to the untreated control ( n = 320, 80.9%). This rate was significantly higher than that of the noncolonized compost mulch ( n = 329, 65.0%, P < 0.001), which showed the highest disease incidence in this cohort. In initially infected vines, the survival rate was higher (but not significantly) under the biocontrol treatment ( n = 50, 54.0%) than in the untreated control ( n = 45, 37.8%), and significantly higher than in the noncolonized compost mulch ( n = 31, 22.6%, P = 0.032). These findings constitute exploratory field evidence that Trichoderma -colonized mulch may mitigate disease progression compared with noncolonized compost mulch, particularly in already symptomatic vines, but replicated field trials are required to confirm treatment efficacy. In addition, the study provides a quantitative framework for the molecular detection and monitoring of A . mellea in woody ecosystems.[Formula: see text] Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). papers.title: Population Genetic Evolution Analysis of Tsaoko Stripe Mosaic Virus and Development of RT-PCR and Real-Time RT-PCR Detection Methods for Strain Discrimination.
papers.abstract: Tsaoko stripe mosaic virus (TkSMV) has been identified as the predominant viral pathogen of Amomum tsaoko in Yunnan Province of China. This virus induced various foliar symptoms, including chlorosis, stripe mosaic, and necrosis, while some infected A. tsaoko plants remain asymptomatic. Comprehensive investigation of the population genetic structure and molecular detection protocols for TkSMV is crucial for elucidating its evolutionary dynamics, epidemiology, and disease control strategies. Phylogenetic analysis based on 15 full-length genomic sequences and 29 coat protein (CP) gene fragments revealed three distinct evolutionary lineages (S1, S2, and S3) within the TkSMV population. Neutrality test analysis indicates that the genetic polymorphism of the TkSMV population is consistent with a neutral evolution model (Tajima's D > 0, not significant). The comparative evolutionary analysis demonstrated significant selective pressures across viral proteins: codon usage bias analysis revealed strong purifying selection (dN/dS < 1) in nine structural/functional proteins, eliminating deleterious mutations. The 9K gene exhibited the highest nucleotide diversity (π = 0.13567), suggesting its role in adaptive evolution. NIa-Pro protease showed the lowest diversity (π = 0.09497), indicating functional constraint. Remarkably, the CP gene displayed polarized evolutionary patterns. The N-terminal region (amino acids 1 to 100) acted as a hypervariable hotspot, while the C-terminal region (amino acids 151 to 240) maintained evolutionary conservation. Furthermore, multiplex RT-PCR assays for accurate discrimination of TkSMV-S1/S2/S3 strains in mixed infections were developed. These advancements provide a technical foundation for epidemiological surveillance through strain-specific monitoring and seed certification programs for A. tsaoko cultivation.

papers.title: A Two-Stage ESM-Based Machine Learning Pipeline for Robust Hierarchically Evaluated Enzyme Function Prediction.
papers.abstract: Accurate enzyme annotation remains a major bottleneck in translating rapidly growing protein sequence data into biological knowledge. Enzyme Commission (EC) prediction is particularly challenging because enzyme functions are organized hierarchically, annotations are often imbalanced across classes, and sequence similarity alone may be insufficient to resolve functional differences. To address these challenges, we developed ESM-ECForest, a 2-stage framework that combines protein embeddings generated by the pretrained language model ESM-2 (Evolutionary Scale Modeling 2) with random forest classifiers. The first stage distinguishes enzymes from nonenzymes, whereas the second assigns one or more EC numbers to proteins predicted to be enzymatic. On an external benchmark comprising 25,778 protein sequences, ESM-ECForest achieved competitive weighted F1 scores among the evaluated off-the-shelf methods, decreasing from 0.94 at Level 1 to 0.90 at Level 4. The largest relative improvements were observed for lyases (EC 4), ligases (EC 6), and translocases (EC 7), although EC 6 and EC 7 remained the most difficult classes internally. Uniform manifold approximation and projection of the ESM-2 embedding space showed clustering patterns that broadly reflected enzyme functional relationships, suggesting that the pretrained representations capture functionally relevant information. These results support the use of pretrained protein language model embeddings as an effective foundation for enzyme annotation. By combining pretrained protein representations with a lightweight supervised classifier, ESM-ECForest provides a scalable approach for EC prediction and may facilitate functional annotation of proteins from large microbial genomic and metagenomic datasets within the taxonomic and EC-label space represented during model development.

papers.title: Evolutionary diversity and structural comparison of the FimA adhesin in Porphyromonas gingivalis.
papers.abstract: Porphyromonas gingivalis is a heterogeneous oral pathogen whose major fimbrial subunit FimA occurs as genotypes linked to adhesion differences. We asked whether fimA diversification tracks the phylogeny, carries selection signatures and varies structurally. We analyzed 99 Porphyromonas assemblies: genotypes were mapped onto the core-genome phylogeny, nucleotide diversity compared with 1248 core genes, recombination screened with GARD, and codon-level selection tested with FEL and MEME, with and without multiple-hit models. Genotype I and IV precursors were characterized by mass spectrometry, SEC-MALS and far-UV circular dichroism; rigid docking used β1-derived peptides and a truncated β1 construct. Genotype was only partially coupled to lineage: 27 tree changes against five expected under clade structure. fimA had Tajima's D = 1.29, 13th of 1247 families, against a negative background; under lineage-balanced sampling of reconstructed alignments its median position fell to the 96th percentile, and within one lineage it was negative. GARD placed two breakpoints and the multiple-hit model fitted better. Ten codons met p ≤ 0.1 for diversifying selection in two or more analyses, none survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction, while 119 to 132 codons met the same nominal threshold for purifying selection and 12 to 18 of those held at q ≤ 0.05. The best supported were V193 and A231, with episodic MEME signals at D52, S55, A76, T227 and A306, and all ten lie outside the mapped epithelial cell-binding region. Both behaved as monomers of 38.3 and 38.0 kDa, their predicted structures superposed at 0.73 Å, and docking gave no convergent interface. The position of fimA depends on the sampling scheme, so these data demonstrate neither balancing nor host-associated selection, and genotype-dependent β1-integrin recognition requires experimental testing.

papers.title: Portable micro-spectrometric LAMP platform for rapid semi-quantitative pathogen detection in food safety.
papers.abstract: This study reports the development of an integrated, portable analytical platform combining a micro-spectrometer with loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for the rapid, on-site detection of Vibrio vulnificus. The system, controlled by LinkIt 7697 microprocessors, achieves precise thermal regulation within ±0.32 °C at 64 °C and features a customized optical path for real-time fluorescence monitoring. Utilizing calcein as a metal-sensitive fluorescent indicator, the device captures the spectral shift and intensity enhancement resulting from the displacement of manganese ions during DNA synthesis. Unlike traditional photodiode-based sensors, the integrated micro-spectrometer enables full-spectrum analysis at 1-minute intervals, providing superior discrimination between true positive signals and background autofluorescence. Experimental results demonstrate successful detection of Vibrio vulnificus genomic fragments within 40 minutes, achieving a detection limit of 0.1 pg/μL, with data automatically synchronized to a cloud database for remote epidemiological surveillance. The combination of high-fidelity spectral acquisition and isothermal chemistry offers a robust, cost-effective solution for food safety monitoring and point-of-care testing in resource-limited environments.

papers.title: Candidozyma auris in intensive care units: A point prevalence study and six-month colonization-infection surveillance.
papers.abstract: Candidozyma auris has emerged as a globally significant nosocomial pathogen due to its multidrug antifungal resistance, environmental persistence, and high mortality rates. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of C. auris colonization through a point prevalence screening in the intensive care units (ICUs) of our hospital and to evaluate colonization and infection outcomes during a subsequent six-month follow-up period. The present study aimed to evaluate C. auris colonization rates through point prevalence screening in the ICUs of our hospital, to assess colonization and infection outcomes during a subsequent six-month follow-up period, and to establish a diagnostic algorithm for C. auris identification in our laboratory. Following the detection of an index C. auris case in our hospital in February 2025, a point prevalence study was conducted in all ICUs. Composite swab samples (bilateral axilla and groin) were obtained from hospitalized patients on the same day. In addition, urine and wound cultures were collected from eligible patients. Isolates were identified using chromogenic media, conventional microbiological methods, and MALDI-TOF MS. After the point prevalence study, surveillance for colonization and bloodstream infection was performed over a six-month period. C. auris colonization was detected in 7 of 70 ICU patients (10%) based on composite swab samples. During the six-month follow-up, colonization was identified in 15 patients, and C. auris fungemia developed in nine patients. All patients with positive blood cultures died. The most frequently identified risk factors were broad-spectrum antibiotic use, prolonged ICU stay, and the presence of urinary catheters. Our findings demonstrate that C. auris colonization can be detected at a high rate in ICUs and that severe invasive infections may develop following colonization. Early diagnosis, active screening strategies, and effective infection control measures are critical for reducing C. auris-associated morbidity and mortality.

papers.title: Phage Cocktail-Mediated Ultrasensitive Real-Time Electrochemical Whole-Cell Detection of Klebsiella pneumoniae on a SPCE.
papers.abstract: Rapid and selective detection of pathogenic bacteria is essential for timely clinical diagnosis and environmental surveillance. In this work, we report a bacteriophage-assisted electrochemical sensing platform for the selective detection of Klebsiella pneumoniae using an Er2O3/Co3O4/Au/polyethylenimine (PEI)-modified screen-printed carbon electrode (SPCE). The hierarchical nanocomposite was engineered to provide high surface area, enhanced charge transfer kinetics, and abundant functional sites for efficient phage immobilization. PEI served as a cationic linker to facilitate electrostatic attachment of lytic bacteriophages while maintaining their biological activity and host specificity. Upon target recognition, phage-bacteria binding at the electrode interface produced pronounced impedance changes due to interfacial blocking and altered electron transfer dynamics. The developed biosensor exhibited high selectivity for Klebsiella pneumoniae over nontarget bacteria and could distinguish live from dead bacteria. The sensor showed a wide linear detection range of 10-107 CFU/mL with a low detection limit of 7.36 CFU/mL and good repeatability with an RSD of ∼1.17%. The real-world applicability of the sensor was tested using aquarium water samples and demonstrated good performance, with recovery percentages ranging from ∼91.71 to 96.26%. This work establishes a robust nano-bio hybrid interface strategy that integrates rare-earth/transition metal oxide electrocatalysts with phage biorecognition on disposable SPCE platforms. The developed system shows strong potential for point-of-care pathogen monitoring in clinical, environmental, and food safety applications.

papers.title: Rapid Detection of Rhizoctonia solani in Turfgrass and Soil Using a Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification-Based Point-of-Care Testing System.
papers.abstract: Climate change is increasing the frequency and scale of turf disease outbreaks, yet systems for rapid and accurate disease diagnosis in the field remain limited. Existing microscopic examination methods require skilled professionals. And by the time visible symptoms appear, the optimal window for prevention is often missed. Rhizoctonia solani is a destructive pathogen causing severe turfgrass diseases. To address this, we report a rapid, field-deployable loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay targeting a fungal-specific ITS-5.8S rDNA sequence. The amplification reaction was optimized at 65 °C for 20 minutes, achieving an analytical sensitivity with a limit of detection (LoD) of 1 fg per reaction. The assay exhibited 100% analytical specificity with no cross-reactivity, validated across a panel of 31 fungal isolates comprising target Rhizoctonia species and non-target taxa, as well as successfully tested on artificially contaminated turf and soil matrices. Overall, this highly sensitive and specific LAMP-based system provides a reliable and practical tool for the rapid, on-site detection of R. solani in turf management.

papers.title: Reliability of using a web-based platform in identifying hereditary cancer syndromes: Analysis of 290 electronically collected pedigrees.
papers.abstract: Identification of hereditary cancer syndromes is difficult in the clinic due to time constraints and evolving professional society recommendations. Several web-based collection systems have been developed, but it is not clear if these tools accurately identify at-risk patients compared to clinical genetic evaluation. This sub-study of the Family History and Cancer Risk Study (FOREST) examines whether web-based collection of family health history (FHH) can reliably identify patients who meet genetic counseling referral guidelines. Participants completed MeTree, a patient-facing web-based FHH collection and clinical decision support tool that generates referral recommendations based on 2015 American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/National Society of Genetic Counselors (ACMG/NSGC) guidelines. MeTree referral classifications were independently reviewed by genetic specialists. Agreement between MeTree and specialist determinations was assessed using Cohen's kappa. Among 288 pedigrees analyzed, 90 (31%) were identified as meeting hereditary cancer referral guidelines. Genetic specialists strongly agreed with 88% (79/90) of MeTree reports with and 99% (196/198) without a referral recommendation (Cohen's Kappa = 0.892). The majority of misclassifications (9 of 13) were due to limitations of data collection of skin cancer sub-types. Scalable patient facing collection systems can reliably identify patients at risk for hereditary cancer syndromes.

papers.title: Direct RNA Targeting by CRISPR/Cas12: Emerging Mechanisms and Diagnostic Applications.
papers.abstract: RNA detection is essential for molecular diagnostics because it provides dynamic information on gene expression, pathogen activity, and disease progression. Conventional RNA detection methods, particularly reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), remain widely used but require RNA-to-DNA conversion, thermal cycling, and relatively complex workflows, limiting their suitability for rapid and point-of-care testing. In CRISPR diagnostics, Cas13 has traditionally been regarded as the major RNA-targeting system, whereas Cas12 enzymes have been primarily recognized as DNA-targeting nucleases. Recent studies, however, have revealed that several Cas12 variants can directly recognize RNA targets, enabling reverse-transcription-free RNA detection through mechanisms such as RNA-triggered DNase activity. In this review, we summarize the emerging functional diversity of RNA-responsive Cas12 systems, including Cas12a, Cas12a2, Cas12a3, Cas12f, and Cas12g, and discuss their underlying mechanisms for direct RNA sensing. We further highlight strategies for enhancing Cas12-mediated RNA detection, including guide and activator engineering, nanomaterial-assisted readouts, and autocatalytic signal amplification. Finally, we discuss its applications in infectious disease diagnosis, cancer biomarker detection, and environmental monitoring, alongside key challenges and future opportunities for clinical translation and point-of-care testing.

papers.title: Beyond Blood Cultures and Echocardiography: Emerging Diagnostics for Infective Endocarditis.
papers.abstract: Management of infective endocarditis (IE) is often confounded by the presence of prosthetic valves, transcatheter prostheses, and cardiovascular implantable electronic devices, as well as by changing epidemiologic risks and antimicrobial resistance patterns. For the diagnosis of IE, blood cultures and echocardiography remain foundational, but important gaps persist, particularly in culture-negative and prosthetic/device-associated infections. Contemporary diagnostic criteria and guidelines now support a multimodality approach incorporating molecular microbiology and advanced imaging. This review summarizes emerging technologies including broad-range 16S/18S/28S rRNA polymerase chain reaction and sequencing, fluorescence in situ hybridization coupled with sequencing, targeted and shotgun metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), plasma microbial cell-free DNA, cardiac computed tomography, and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography/computed tomography. We also examine the potential role of artificial intelligence in echocardiographic interpretation and of large language models in multimodal data integration. Current evidence suggests that tissue-based molecular testing generally provides greater microbiologic yield than valve culture in culture-negative IE, while blood-based mNGS and microbial cell-free DNA may extend pathogen detection after antibiotic exposure and reduce reliance on tissue-based diagnosis. However, heterogeneity in specimen handling, sequencing pipelines, contamination control, reporting thresholds, and clinical interpretation remains a major barrier to implementation. Future progress should move beyond pathogen detection toward rapid, reproducible, clinically actionable diagnosis that integrates organism identification, anatomic localization, disseminated disease, and personalized treatment. Prospective outcome trials, standardized workflows, cost-effectiveness studies, and multidisciplinary Endocarditis Team integration can help determine whether these technologies translate into better antimicrobial stewardship, procedural decision-making, and patient outcomes.

papers.title: The application of proteomics in asthma research: a bibliometric analysis.
papers.abstract: Asthma is a common inflammatory disease of the respiratory system. Following the advent of genomics, proteomics has emerged as a valuable research approach. This study aimed to pinpoint key research areas and trends in the use of proteomics for asthma through bibliometric analysis, offering insights into future research paths. Articles related to asthma and proteomics published between 2000 and 2024 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. The data were analyzed and visualized using the bibliometric software CiteSpace (version number: v.6.1 R6). A total of 520 articles were included in this study, and a gradual increase in the annual publication volume was observed. The USA, China, and Sweden ranked as the top three countries in terms of publication output. The USA exhibited the highest centrality (0.42), indicating its influence in this field. At the institutional level, the Karolinska Institute had the highest number of publications. The keyword clustering analysis revealed that the research focuses on airway inflammation mechanisms, proteomics methodologies, precision medicine applications, and clinical phenotype characterization. Keywords like "proteomics," "mass spectrometry," and "precision medicine" have seen significant citation increases recently, highlighting proteomics' role in advancing asthma research, biomarker discovery, and personalized therapies. By systematically examining the application and development of proteomics in the field of asthma research via a bibliometric analysis, we have generated a comprehensive knowledge framework for researchers. Future studies should place greater emphasis on the clinical application of biomarkers, multi-omics integration, and the development of personalized treatment strategies.

papers.title: Europium nanoparticle-based lateral flow assay for rapid detection of herpes simplex virus 2-specific antibodies in serum: a preliminary evaluation.
papers.abstract: Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) is a widely prevalent human pathogen responsible for the majority of genital herpes infections. Type-specific serological screening is a valuable approach for identifying asymptomatic individuals who may unknowingly transmit HSV to sexual partners and neonates, and can inform prevention, treatment, and vaccination strategies aimed at reducing transmission. Here, we describe the development and preliminary evaluation of a Europium nanoparticle-based lateral flow assay (EuNP-LFA) for rapid detection of HSV-2-specific immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies in human serum within 10 minutes. Preliminary performance evaluation using a commercially available anti-herpes mixed-titer performance panel demonstrated 90% sensitivity and 90.9% specificity relative to the FDA-cleared HerpeSelect™ HSV-2 ELISA reference classification. Receiver operating characteristic analysis yielded an area under the curve of 0.918 (95% CI: 0.688-0.983), indicating good discriminatory performance in this preliminary dataset. These findings support the feasibility of the EuNP-LFA as a proof-of-concept platform for rapid HSV-2 serological testing and support further evaluation in larger, clinically representative specimen populations to establish its diagnostic performance and potential utility for point-of-care applications.

papers.title: Metax enables accurate cross-domain taxonomic profiling of metagenomes.
papers.abstract: Taxonomic profiling is fundamental to microbiome research, yet achieving high species-level accuracy remains challenging for complex communities that span bacteria, viruses, eukaryotes, and archaea, and these limitations are exacerbated in low-biomass, host-dominated samples. We introduce Metax, a cross-domain taxonomic profiler that integrates coverage-based probabilistic modeling with an expectation-maximization framework to distinguish true microbial signals from artifacts. Across >600 samples from host-associated, environmental, wastewater, and low-biomass clinical settings, including benchmarks with limited reference representation, Metax improved profiling accuracy, achieving on average 55% higher F1 scores and 45% lower Bray-Curtis dissimilarity than other methods. Moreover, this broad evaluation demonstrated that Metax resolved bacterial and viral signatures of peri-implantitis in oral microbiomes and revealed signals suggestive of reagent-borne contaminants and reference misassemblies in plasma-cell-free DNA. By leveraging genome-wide coverage evidence, Metax enables robust cross-domain profiling across diverse sample types and sequencing depths, including settings where reference databases are highly incomplete.

papers.title: Transcriptome analysis of mRNA and long non-coding RNA profiles in the brains of CVA10-infected suckling mice.
papers.abstract: Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) caused by Coxsackievirus A10 (CVA10) remains an important public health concern. Although most infections are self-limiting, severe cases may develop neurological complications, including acute flaccid paralysis and aseptic meningitis. However, host transcriptional responses to CVA10 infection within the central nervous system (CNS) remain poorly understood. Here, we established a CVA10-infected ICR suckling mouse model and performed transcriptomic profiling of brain tissues using RNA-seq, followed by RT-qPCR validation. A total of 243 differentially expressed mRNAs and 776 differentially expressed lncRNAs were identified in the brains of CVA10-infected mice. Interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as Ifit1 exhibited significant dysregulation in CVA10-infected brain tissue. Integrated GO and KEGG functional enrichment analyses revealed that these genes were significantly associated with innate immune and inflammatory responses, particularly interferon-related signaling pathways. Protein-protein interaction network analysis identified ten immune-related hub genes, including Irf7, Rsad2, Isg15, Stat1, Ifih1, Ifit1, Ifit3, Oasl2, Rtp4 and Usp18. RT-qPCR validation showed overall agreement with RNA-seq findings, supporting the reliability of the transcriptomic analysis. Long non coding RNAs can extensively regulate these immune-related genes in both directions. These results offer a foundation for further investigation of the molecular basis of CVA10-related neurological disease, and for exploring candidate biomarkers and molecular targets.

papers.title: Identification and prognostic value of non-hotspot POLE exonuclease domain mutations in endometrial cancer.
papers.abstract: Endometrial cancer with somatic POLE exonuclease domain mutations (EDMs) has a highly favorable prognosis; however, the clinical implications of non-hotspot EDMs in POLE remain unclear. In 793 patients with endometrial cancer enrolled at the National Cancer Center and Juntendo University Hospitals, 25 prespecified variants were screened using the Luminex assay. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was carried out to evaluate 54 patients with hotspot and non-hotspot EDMs. In patients with endometrial cancer (n = 4864) registered in Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (GENIE), those harboring hotspot EDMs were matched with randomly sampled patients without EDMs, and a polymerase epsilon (POLE) score for gene panel testing was developed. In our cohort, POLE-EDMs, including hotspot (n = 91) and non-hotspot (n = 12) EDMs, were identified in 103 (12.9%) of 793 patients. The prevalence of grade 3 and advanced-stage endometrial cancer was higher in patients with non-hotspot EDMs than in those with hotspot EDMs. WES analysis of 54 patients revealed no significant differences in genomic mutations between the groups, and four non-hotspot EDMs were identified. A POLE-specific mutational signature was observed in tumors with EDM. In addition, the POLE score criteria were developed based on hotspot EDMs using the GENIE cohort, achieving a detection sensitivity of 0.94. Using the established POLE score, we identified nine non-hotspot EDMs. We identified 13 novel candidate non-hotspot EDMs using a newly established POLE score for gene panels and demonstrated an association between non-hotspot EDMs and favorable prognosis. The identification of additional non-hotspot EDMs will facilitate precise molecular classification of endometrial cancer.

papers.title: Computational and experimental study of CuO-ZnO nanocomposite using the plant Peganum harmala L. and their antifungal, antibacterial applications.
papers.abstract: The rapid emergence of AMR necessitates the development of novel, sustainable therapeutic agents. This study reports the green synthesis of copper-decorated zinc oxide (CuO-ZnO) nanocomposite using an aqueous leaf extract of Peganum harmala L., which served as a reducing and capping agent. A quantitative EDX analysis confirmed a high loading of Cu of 24.25% (7.09%) mass. Characterization showed that the average primary particle size was 29 ± 1.3 nm, and that the structures were crystalline and hexagonal, known as wurtzite. The nanocomposite exhibited a positive zeta potential of + 47.2 ± 4.24 mV, indicating good colloidal stability. A typical absorption peak at 372 nm was observed using UV-visible spectroscopy. The CuO-ZnO nanocomposite showed significant dose-dependent antibacterial activity with Minimum Inhibitory Concentrations (MIC) of 50 µg/mL, 70 µg/mL, and 80 µg/mL for Staphylococcus epidermidis, Salmonella typhi, and Klebsiella pneumoniae, respectively. The synthesized CuO-ZnO nanocomposite exhibited significant antifungal activity, inhibiting the linear growth of Aspergillus flavus and Fusarium oxysporum by 87.67 mm and 74.33 mm, respectively. While computational models suggest localized structural integration, the system is described as a copper-decorated zinc oxide network, pending high-resolution phase-state verification. This integrated study highlights the potential of P. harmala-mediated CuO-ZnO nanocomposite as an eco-friendly antimicrobial agent for biomedical applications.

papers.title: Detection of high-risk sequence type ST131 among multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli causing urinary tract infections in Cusco, Peru.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli represents a growing public health challenge, particularly in urinary tract infections (UTIs), where this pathogen remains the leading etiological agent. The emergence of multidrug-resistant strains producing extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) and carbapenemases has markedly limited therapeutic options and promoted the persistence of high-risk lineages in hospital settings. In this study, phenotypic, molecular, and genomic characterization were conducted on 50 multidrug-resistant (MDR) E. coli isolates obtained from urine cultures of patients treated at the Regional Hospital of Cusco, Peru. ESBL and carbapenemase production were assessed using standardised phenotypic methods, while resistance genes were detected by endpoint PCR. For genomic characterization, MDR E. coli isolates (RUE 08 and RUE 29) were selected from the panel of 50 isolates. These were chosen as representative samples for whole-genome sequencing and comparative genomic analysis. All isolates were confirmed as ESBL producers, and 40% exhibited carbapenemase production. The detected genes were bla CTX-M (94%), bla TEM (36%), bla SHV (2%), bla NDM (26%), bla OXA-48 (20%) and bla KPC was not detected. The detection of bla NDM and bla OXA-48 represents the first documented report of these genes in multidrug-resistant E. coli in the city of Cusco. Genomic analysis identified the high-risk lineage ST131 in one sequenced isolate, characterised by an extensive repertoire of virulence and resistance genes associated with the ExPEC/UPEC pathotype, as well as a second isolate belonging to ST361, which harboured clinically relevant resistance genes but displayed a limited virulence profile.
